🧨 The New Middle East. Israel Isn’t In It

On February 28, 2026, when the joint US–Israeli strikes on Iran began, Netanyahu promised one thing: Israel helps break the Shia axis, America crowns it as the new regional center, and alliances form around Jerusalem. 

Iran’s known nuclear sites were dismantled, Khamenei was killed and replaced within a day by his son Mojtaba, Hezbollah’s leadership was hit — the axis took a real blow. But the political endgame went elsewhere.

The Islamabad memorandum was agreed in mid‑June as a 60‑day framework: reopen Hormuz to commercial shipping, ease the US blockade, and negotiate over Iran’s nuclear and missile programs. Netanyahu admitted he did not know its full text and Israel was nowhere near the table. 

In July, after renewed US strikes and new American casualties, Iran publicly suspended its commitments, Washington went back to nightly waves of attacks, and the Hormuz crisis returned. Israel was excluded from a deal that then fell apart, while the regional rearrangement carried on without it.

That is the backdrop for the July moves. On July 7, Trump lifted sanctions on Turkey and opened the way to F‑35s despite Israeli objections. 

On July 21–22, he approved a 30‑year civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that gives Riyadh a conditional right to enrich uranium without demanding recognition of Israel. 

The Saudi deal allows an enrichment plant if a future joint study finds domestic fuel economically justified, with no blanket ban on enrichment and no requirement for the IAEA Additional Protocol. 

It doesn’t bring a Saudi bomb closer tomorrow; it rewrites the rules of who gets US nuclear tech and on what terms.

Three old exchanges snap at once. The atom‑for‑recognition bargain is gone: Saudis get nuclear status without normalizing with Israel. 

The tech‑for‑no‑enrichment “gold standard” becomes just one precedent the UAE once accepted: after Riyadh’s softer terms, new customers will start from the Saudi baseline, not the Emirati one. And the Israeli “no” stops being a structural veto: big US decisions on Turkey and Saudi Arabia are now made over Israel’s head.

Around that, a new architecture emerges. Riyadh buys status and autonomy; Pakistan sells mediation between Washington and Tehran; Turkey builds capability with Russian, Western and Asian help. 

The strikes that broke Iran’s program didn’t end the nuclear story in the region; they changed its cast. For years, Israel mattered because it was the main route into Washington and the hinge of regional deals. After July, that route increasingly runs around it.

The new Middle East is taking shape — just not by Israel, and not for it.
